strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: converting dense LLMs to MoE architectures without the substantial cost of continual pre-training that prior conversion methods (LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2) require.

The router construction is derived analytically from a clearly stated optimization objective (matching MoE output to dense FFN output), giving the method a principled foundation rather than being purely heuristic.

The balanced clustering formulation (reduction of unbalanced to balanced linear assignment) is a reasonable and clearly explained technical contribution for grouping co-activated neurons into routed experts.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided: calibration data size, fine-tuning data size vs. construction time trade-off, load-balancing effectiveness, expert configuration choices, and a scaling check to a 13B model.
Comparisons against LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 show CMoE is dramatically more usable in the training-free regime (baselines produce NaN/very high PPL), and after light fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The headline claim of "lossless precision" at 75% activation is not well supported by the data: Table 1 shows training-free PPL of 7.02 vs. dense 5.27 on WikiText-2 (a ~33% relative degradation) and even after fine-tuning, PPL (5.69) still exceeds dense (5.27); similar gaps appear on C4. This overstatement appears in the abstract, contributions, and conclusion and is a significant discrepancy between claims and evidence.

The "76% downstream accuracy recovery" claim is not representative: Table 2 shows this figure applies mainly to SciQ/BoolQ at 25% activation, while other tasks (e.g., HellaSwag, ARC-C) show much larger degradation (e.g., HellaSwag 38.79 vs. dense 78.55, roughly 50% recovery), so the headline number appears selectively reported rather than reflecting overall performance.

Reported inference speedups are modest and somewhat inconsistent with the framing of the paper as an acceleration method: at 75% activation (where quality is closest to dense), full-model speedup is only 1.05x–1.12x, undermining the practical value proposition at the higher-quality operating point.

No comparison against simpler competitive baselines for the same efficiency goal (e.g., structured FFN pruning + light fine-tuning, or contextual sparsity methods like Deja Vu already cited), making it hard to assess whether the added complexity of MoE conversion is justified relative to simpler alternatives with comparable training-free/lightweight-tuning cost.

Several of the underlying approximations (e.g., Eq. 3's hypothesis that |h_i w_down,i| ≈ |h_i| justifying neuron-independent activation scoring) are validated only qualitatively via a single-layer/single-token histogram in Appendix A rather than systematically across layers, models, and tasks.

Missing experimental/reporting details: hardware specifications and batch sizes for the memory-bound vs. compute-bound latency measurements are not clearly specified, no variance/seed information is given, and the code repository link is blank in the provided manuscript, limiting reproducibility verification.
Writing quality issues are present (e.g., duplicated text "modifies [12] modifies," garbled text "oo deease" in the SliceGPT description), suggesting the manuscript needs additional proofreading.

The comparison against LLaMA-MoE/LLaMA-MoE-v2 in the fully training-free setting may be somewhat unfair, since those methods were designed under the assumption of subsequent continual pre-training/post-training rather than for direct training-free deployment; their catastrophic collapse may partly reflect this mismatch rather than a fundamental limitation relative to CMoE.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation (bimodal neuron activation-frequency distribution) that directly informs the method design, distinguishing it conceptually from prior weight-based clustering approaches.

Broad experimental coverage: four base models spanning 7B-30B parameters (plus a 72B model for speedup evaluation), five zero-shot benchmarks, and additional knowledge/coding/math evaluations (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K).

Extensive and informative ablations: calibration source/size sensitivity, isolating the contribution of clustering vs. routing (Table 5), load-balancing effects, orthogonality with neuron-level activation sparsity (WINA), self-consistency behavior, and expert configuration sensitivity.

Strong practical value proposition: restructuring completes in minutes with only a few thousand calibration/fine-tuning samples versus hundreds of billions of tokens for prior FFN-to-MoE approaches, which is a meaningful systems-level contribution.
The analytical router derivation, while approximate, is clearly laid out with explicit assumptions (Appendix A.1-A.4), aiding reproducibility of the core algorithm.
Demonstrated applicability both to dense models and recursively to existing MoE models (hierarchical sparsity), broadening the scope of applicability.
weaknesses: The central sparsity hypothesis (arg min|h_i w_i| ≈ arg min|h_i|, Eq. 12) ignores the magnitude of w_i entirely and is not empirically validated (e.g., no measurement of how well hidden-state magnitude alone predicts true output contribution); this weakens the theoretical grounding of the analytical router.

Reported speedups are modest and inconsistent with the FLOPs reduction claims: while FLOPs drop by ~16-18%, actual throughput/latency gains range from near-zero (1.02x) up to 1.17x only in a cherry-picked best-case compute-bound, long-context configuration, which could overstate practical impact if headlined as the main efficiency result.

Some baseline results appear implausibly weak (e.g., LLaMA-MoE achieving near-random accuracy on several tasks after fine-tuning), raising concerns about whether baselines originally designed for large-scale continual pretraining were fairly adapted to the paper's low-data regime, potentially inflating the apparent margin of improvement.
No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported gains, especially for closely-spaced ablation comparisons.

Wall-clock/throughput numbers appear to be measured under a specific (unspecified in detail) implementation/hardware setup; reproducibility of the exact speedup figures is unclear without more implementation detail or released code.

The method is specifically tailored to SwiGLU-style gated FFNs; generalization to other FFN variants, encoder-decoder, or non-transformer architectures is left entirely to future work, limiting the demonstrated scope of the contribution.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to MoEfication/EMoE/G-MoEfication — the core idea (separating high-frequency neurons into shared experts, analytical router from representative neurons) is a natural extension of known sparsity structure rather than a conceptually new mechanism.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated empirical observation (bimodal neuron activation-frequency distribution, Figure 2) that directly informs the proposed shared/routed expert partition, and is validated for domain invariance via cross-domain overlap analysis (math/science/code).

Broad experimental coverage: four model families spanning 7B to 70B/30B-A3B parameters, five zero-shot benchmarks plus MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, and an industrial-scale speedup evaluation on Qwen-2.5 72B.

Careful, apples-to-apples baseline comparison: all MoE-restructuring baselines are re-implemented and fine-tuned under the same 2k-sample budget, isolating the contribution of the analytical construction itself rather than confounding it with data budget differences.

Thorough ablations that decompose the method's gains: Table 5 separately varies clustering strategy and router construction, showing both the activation-based shared/routed partition and the analytical router each contribute independently; additional ablations cover calibration source/size, load balancing, expert configuration, and orthogonality with neuron-level sparsity (WINA) and quantization-adjacent techniques.

Practical efficiency validation beyond accuracy: FLOPs/MACs/throughput measurements, real end-to-end conversion time (minutes vs. weeks/days for retraining baselines), and compute-/memory-bound speedup across context lengths, which strengthens the deployment relevance of the claims.

The training-free variant already substantially outperforms fine-tuned baselines (Table 3), supporting the central claim that the analytical construction—not the fine-tuning—drives most of the improvement, which is a meaningful and testable claim well-supported by evidence.
weaknesses: The central 'sparsity hypothesis' underlying the analytical router (Eq. 12, argmin|h_i w_i| ≈ argmin|h_i|) ignores variation in the magnitude of w_down,i across neurons and is justified only by a vague appeal to small ||F(x)|| from residual connections; no direct empirical quantification of the approximation's tightness (e.g., correlation between |h_i| ranking and actual output-norm contribution ranking) is provided, leaving the theoretical core somewhat heuristic despite downstream accuracy gains.

Reported speedups are fairly modest (up to 1.17x, mostly 1.05–1.15x) relative to the 16–18% FLOPs reduction and the substantial machinery introduced (clustering, analytical router, LoRA fine-tuning, load balancing); the paper does not deeply analyze why FLOPs savings only partially translate to wall-clock/throughput gains, nor discuss when this trade-off is/is not worthwhile.

Accuracy-speed configurations are inconsistent across tables (e.g., main accuracy results use S3A3E8 while the best reported speedup uses S1A5E8), making it hard to assess the simultaneous accuracy-speedup trade-off for any single fixed configuration.

No variance/error bars across multiple runs or seeds are reported, despite the paper's own discussion of routing-induced generation variance (Section 5.4, self-consistency results) and stochastic LoRA fine-tuning—this weakens confidence in the statistical reliability of reported gains, especially the smaller ablation deltas.

Noticeable accuracy degradation on harder tasks remains at the primary evaluated sparsity level (e.g., ARC-Challenge drops ~6 points on Llama-2 7B at 25% sparsity), and the paper does not thoroughly characterize where the accuracy-efficiency trade-off becomes unfavorable for practical deployment.

The intriguing claim that the converted model slightly outperforms the dense baseline at low sparsity (Table 10, 'implicit regularization') is based on a single perplexity data point without further investigation or statistical support, and risks being an artifact of fine-tuning noise rather than a genuine phenomenon.

No clear code/artifact release is evidenced in the visible manuscript text (footnote reference present but content not shown), which affects independent reproducibility verification despite otherwise detailed methodological description.
